blocks.x: I'm L.D. Harris. My real name is Lawrence Douglas Harris. I was born and raised in Brenham, Texas. That's about 165 miles from here. It's on H and T.C. between Austin and Houston, Texas. And I started out playing music between the ages of 13 and 14, started studying music. They organized a boys band there. I had a fellow who had been in the service by the name of Gus Allen. Everybody called him Uncle Beansy. He's quite a musician. And my father and several other fathers there in the city thought it would be a good thing for the boys to organize a band there. Something to keep us off the street, I guess, keep us out of the devil. So they did, and they put me on the alto horn. And I worked from that alto horn to the valve trombone. And then I got ambitious and wanted to play the slide trombone. And I went off and played the slide trombone. It got to be pretty good. And every summer, after I got about 15 years old, every summer from then on until I was about 18, my father would let me go down to Houston and play with Sid Isles. Sid Isles had this whole southwest tied up. He was from Texas, all Texas, part of Louisiana, New Mexico, tied up. He just mentioned his name and that was it. He'd get a crowd. And he let me go down and play with him. Well, I learned the business of managing a band and how to lead a bunch of fellas and learn something about. In those days, they had, the bands were kind of on a, you had brass bands or players. John Johnson.
John Johnson. You want to go there one time?

Yeah. I want to get that myself up. Well, now, let's see. I was telling you about going down to Houston there. And I learned to lead a bunch of fellas, what the responsibilities was. I did pretty good after that. I got started. And I went off with a, left here, left Sid Isles, and went off with a carnival, carnival show. The boys said they were going down to Mexico, and I'd never been to Mexico, and I wanted to get away and go down to Mexico. So I just forgot about school, went on down there. The old man Sid Isles, well, he had promised the old man to take care of me like a father, which he did. I lived right in the house with him there. And he wouldn't give me my clothes. And the only way I could get my clothes, I had to write a letter and put it inside another envelope and tell the boy, a friend of mine, when you get this, to mail it to the old man, tell him I'm at home. So he'll send my clothes home. I sent them home to my mother. I got my mother to send them to me after he sent them home to me. So that's where I got my clothes down in Mexico. I stayed down there now. I made good down around the border. I got my mother to call them down this border right now. Texas Valley down there. So I came on back, back Houston again, got buried with Houston again. And we organized a band there called Alexander's Ragtime Jazz Band. Old Dave Alexander. We named it after him. He was well known. He worked on the ice truck, well known a lot of people, a lot of people, a lot of them, kind of felt like they keep you laughing all the time. About what year was that? That was long about 1921. Yeah, about 21, maybe about 1920. Anyway, we all got this band and we got lots of work. We just went to clean up around there. About stuff We were playing down there for Don Roby. He had this place, what's the name of that place, Don? Harlem Grill. Harlem Grill. He was operating this Harlem Grill and we head out playing down there. We closed Duke up.

It's alright when the red light go on. Go ahead. When the red light would go on then you start to recording. Now the man in the back that's recording it, there was a little light thread would come off of that disc and it would pile up and then you'd have to wrap it up and take it off and throw it on the floor. And that was one continuous operation until you cut the disc and then the lights would go on and nobody said a word, nothing dropped on the floor, you couldn't breathe too hard. That's right. Today it's a lot different.
That's the way it was now we made our first records. We were so crazy about the records we even saved that little, that little shave in it. And I kept that for a long time.
Look at that I made records, you don't believe it?

Yeah. I tell you another fellow was going good then when Dave had his band, a fellow by the name of Frank Davis. He was a drummer, marvelous drummer. And well Frank was getting a lot of work too and we were young and new in the business and Frank would get so much work he couldn't do it, he would throw it our way. That helped us to keep getting a lot of work too. And I remember making a picture, I never get to see that picture. They showed it there at the Queen Theater there in Houston. And we went out to this place called Camp Kilke. Mr. Kirby and his son-in-law Mr. Ratcliffe had a big summer resort out there. I don't know. I don't know whether that was a river or what that was, a big body of water out there. About 30, 40 miles out between Houston and Galveston. And they had yachts and everything, bowling clubs and everything. People just go down there and stay for weekends. And I had a fellow by the name of Jim Wiley who was colored Stewart and ran the place. And whatever deal you made with Stewart, that was it. He paid off. We'd go down there and play three or four days at a time and stay right there in the place and eat and drink and sleep and play. I made this picture. At that time there were four governors attending this party that I played there. If I can remember it was Governor Neff, Governor Hall, Governor Ferguson, and I can't remember the other ones. Four governors were there at the time. I guess it must have been, maybe it must have been Governor Ferguson was the governor and he was impeaching his wife. That's right, tomorrow Ferguson. Tomorrow Ferguson was the governor. So I guess that's where he was. But anyway, the four governors there. And movie stars and everything. Well that kind of publicity just put us smack over man. We just went like wildfire. So after we got it going so strong, old Davis says, look here, we used to use his name. We'll get on the case of court. We'll say, hey, what's your name? We didn't ask you for your name in place. Well he got over it all right. We kept on playing. And I came on over here to back over here to Waco. I got with a bunch.
Oh yeah. Well when I left there I left there with Ida Cox.

Incidentally I see where she gotta write up where she stuff Yeah, she cut out and cut some records again. I'd like to hear that. I played for her. And that little boy out of Houston, I don't know if you remember him, dog, my name was Skinny, he couldn't read but he could play the best piano player ever in my life. He was really terrific.

Well it seemed in those days, I'll say from the early 20s to the first to the 30s, most of the piano players, they didn't read. You take in New Orleans, Paul, there were a number of piano players while they couldn't read but played so terrific piano.
And the chords were perfect. You can check them today and the chords were right, it was great.

The guy that left here, Edgar Perry, call him Edgar, Edgar Perry. He had a tremendous, a royal garden band. Royal garden band. Edgar Perry, he was a terrific pianist. I couldn't read a note. No. And so many others. I mean I could name the fellas that I knew around at it, terrific musicians that couldn't read. Well you take for instance the pianist that Pihon had so long, Steve Lewis. Well Steve was, I imagine you recall some of his recordings if you heard them. Well Steve was sincere. I just heard it. He was sincere. Yeah.

Sure he was. Well I got over there at Wickle and I got with George Carver's band, they were all readers, George could read. We did very good with that band. And while I was there, Wardell, well I'm cutting out a lot of it because I had gone up to Omeon Nebraska and had a band of my own up there in Omeon Nebraska. And I ran into this guy, Nat Tolles. Nat Tolles, he's still on there.
He is from New Orleans. Yeah and Buster and a whole bunch of musicians up there. He is from New Orleans.

And I stayed with there about three years. I played Omeon Nebraska in there. Played in the grotto. But I stayed in my long time. I stayed in the grotto. But I stayed in my long time. I stayed in the grotto. And I stayed in the grotto. And I stayed in the grotto. I was in the plantation garden. I was in South Park.

The thing that Paul doesn't know too much about you that I want to give to him. I think the part that he's most interested in is this. Of course all of the background from bringing it up to date is fine. Bringing it up to date is fine. But he recalls hearing the solo that you played with Boots and his buddies on Cherry. Isn't that correct Paul? So I imagine that that is part of the thing that Paul would like to answer.
Perhaps that's most thing he's interested in.
That and I want to ask you to tell me a little later about Lazy Daddy.
Oh yeah.
I know a question that I play with. Yes that's correct.

I'll play with it. Well then I came out on the house and came on down here and organized a band again in Temple, Texas. I stayed there and while I was there Boots had played with me in Houston and he heard that I was in Temple and Walter Wardell was here organizing the band. Boots told him, I know a way you can get a good first man, a clean tone, nice player. So let's try to get him. Several guys have been trying to get me down here. He brought my hometown, Jack Rampson. He's been trying to get me down here. A lot of guys. But I was doing pretty good in my own little outfit up there in Temple. They didn't have no competition so I stayed there. But I knew sooner or later the town was too small and I wanted to spread out and get bigger I'd have to leave. So when Walter they came up there, talked to me, told my wife, I said, I think I'll take them up. I told her what the deal was. She ran the band for six weeks till I came down here and rehearsed with this guy to try it out. We didn't play a single job for six weeks so I told them, I said, if we don't get some work, I'm going on back to my outfit. So they flew around. Anyway, I stayed with Waddell, they finally got some work, I stayed with Waddell until that band busted up and looked like the same thing happened there that Don C. had trouble with Troy. The money was going one way and I didn't like that going the wrong way.
What year did you join Boots' band when you cut those records? Was that somewhere in the 30s?
Yeah. In 1932 we got that band together, the last part of the 32.
Now that's the year that I was in Buffalo, New York. Yeah. Now you cut those records here in San Antonio?

No, we didn't cut the records till 33. I got to organize the band in 32. And we cut the band in 33, cut the records rather in 33, cut that Waddell Sharers. We made three sides, I think we made three sides and they put something else on the other side. And out of the two records we got three sides. And Wild Cherry was one of them.
Okay. Well that's the record, I mean that is the part.

Well that's the record that made Boots and that's the record of course that made me and myself at the same time made Boots. We had no idea that was going to be a hit. I'll tell you how that came about. We had some music there with this tune Cherry, they called it Cherry but it was written so doggone high it was still up around C and above all the time. Really we couldn't play it. Didn't have anybody in the band could reach those high notes except the third man and he couldn't have the first. And I could make, I could hit those notes but I couldn't play up there. Well they were going to have rehearsal at my house and Sy Kye Collins, this boy that had played with Troy, had cut out from Troy's band and came over to Boots' band and he took
up with me, he liked to hang around my house all the time.

We'd always get our horns out and sit around there puff and blow, just bow and set without any piano coming or anything. He'd sit there and blow. He'd blow something, I'd blow something. Enjoyed that. So before rehearsal we got home out of that day and I started playing around this thing Cherry. Well I blew till my lips, my lips was chopped and was gone and my chops was gone and I'd come back downstairs and I went to play and instead of making it like they had it written I'd come and put my lip in it. And he says, do that again. Well I did it, when I got to do it again, well he hit the bridge, he took the bridge, he takes that bridge, goes on through it and I took it again. He says, you know that sounds good like that. He said, how about we just, let's take it down again. I said, okay, you like that?
He said, man, I think it stinks. He said, no, that sounds good, you want some handle?
Well all right, when Booth came I had wrote an arrangement on Tiger Rag, well I insisted on him playing, let's play this Tiger. Tip

He said, yeah man, but let him play what he's been playing today on this thing. We had no record on the music. We said, oh man, we've got some stocks here we've got to run over. Finally they got around to it. He said, let him play it man. Well they played it, the guy said, yeah man, that thing is crazy. Well they all fell in and got the harmony and everything. Well they went back and got this arrangement, oh wait a minute, listen to what this chord is here. Well we used some of the same chords in this thing, in this arrangement, but we played it maybe slower, instead of this thing was fast and screaming, one of those screaming was the right chords, you know. He used to write music to kill the brass, you know. Well I changed that all around, see. I changed the darn thing, I almost changed the melody, you know. So they liked it. When Oberstein heard it, he said, that's an original. So I said, well where did you get that song? I got my idea, Cherries. He said, well you can't call that Cherries too, they're not the same number. It's a different tempo, it's a different mood. When I went right away, when I was talking, I didn't know he was an experienced musician, he was talking about the moods and the movements, and it's all right. He did. He changed. Made the record of it, played it back. It sounded terrific man, it was good, it didn't sound like the same.
It can't be, play it again.

So I listened to it. That was it. Well when he got through he came to me, he says, or he went to Boots, he says, Boots, who's number is that? I was looking around. He says, L.D., he says, I did. I said, well I don't know. Somebody's got a claiming number. I said, I don't know. I just, well okay, it's my number. I said, what's your name? He says, these guy's writing. My name was Lawrence Douglas Harris. I said, well what if I said L.D.? My name was L.D., I said, I don't know what's your name. I said, well that's too long. I said, well that's too long. At that time, Joe was the popular name of the guy. I asked him to go to the guy. I asked him to go to the guy. I asked him to go to the guy. I asked him to go to the guy. At that time Joe was the popular name, all the musicians, they called him Joe. Somebody, Troy, no I wasn't Troy, Jimmy Lusford had made a number of, Joe plays and so and so in the band. The name Joe stuck to the musicians. Everybody wanted to be called Joe. I said Joe Harris. Okay, that's all right, Joe Harris was new. Well he wrote Joe Harris. And that's on the record right today. Pooch and his buddies, Joe Harris of course. I don't know how much I got out of it.
It wasn't too much in those days. You know it, what? I know what I got out of mine.

But I mean playing it, that was a kick. That was a thousand dollars right back. Sure. Guys would ask me, how does it feel to walk up and drop a liquor in a jukebox and hear yourself play? I said oh man, there's nothing to it but hell I was thrilling inside you know. It was thrilling inside.
Well you mentioned a great man, the Lazy Daddy, any particular thing you would like to know about him?
Well just tell me a little bit how you played and you mentioned that, what did you say that his real name was? Henry Fillmore.
Well did he do anything else besides play piano? That's about all I ever know. Well we wouldn't want to mention his sideline.
I don't think it would be too bad. He lived and put in all my life. He might have drank once in a while. But he liked the ladies down there especially in the office in those times.

But Lazy Daddy was a very, very lovable fellow. He always had a pleasant word for everyone. I can't recall seeing him mad with anyone. And the trumpet player that left Troy's band that I succeeded in was one of the finest trumpet men I have ever heard and that's saying a lot. That was Claude Beno Kennedy. You've heard talk of him. He didn't last long enough to really imprint his name but he was a terrific trumpet player. And he joined Lazy Daddy's band to show Troy up, Troy Floyd's band, and come here doing it. But he passed just a few months, about a year or so later after he left Troy's band.

Yeah they had a terrific band. And Henry stayed there in Houston for years. Henry was the type of musician that it was, it's amazing how he could do it. He couldn't read. And those shows would come in there. Well those shows would come down from Chicago and New York. Houston used to be a great theatrical town for Vaudeville and stuff like that. So they played a lot of them and I played them too. And we'd always like to get Henry because Henry could play that show down. Well you mean Lazy Daddy. Yeah.
He was in the film. Yeah. Lazy Daddy.

Play that show right down. And he couldn't read but the keys didn't mean anything to us who could read a little bit, keys would give us trouble. The keys didn't mean anything because some guys said well if this guy can't read he can play the keys we can't play. I said well because he doesn't know it's hard.
Yeah it's like I said those days it was a trend for piano players not to read. I guess so.
They didn't read much. They didn't read.

In fact I don't remember too many of them that I played with until I got my band and Al Freeman really read music he could even transpose to that site. And he saved me but I know of so many piano players that wouldn't even attempt to look at a sheet of music. But they could still play like L.D. says in every key, play everything, no missing note. Well Eddie Hayward's daddy, I knew him personally. I sat in a pit with him in Atlanta, Georgia. He was another great piano player that could conceive an idea in his head and bring it out without looking at a sheet.

Talking about sheets though, we're getting away from Lazy Daddy but the guy, the most terrific guy I could, I don't know where I could do anything with sheets, taking my sheet out of my mind, I thought about writing music when he said sheet, was Lester Young's father, old man Billy Young. I played in his band. And you know just like we're sitting here talking, he keeps the conversation going and writing the parts. He said, you didn't write a cue sheet, just sit down and write the part. He might write the cue sheet after he gets through. But he's writing the parts. He'll take that run over, dog. He'll take that cross over, we're going to play this tonight, so and so and so and so. Watch that part right down there in the B right there in the letter so and so and so. It was difficult that time. That's where he wrote the music, just like you're writing a letter. Terrific old man. I worked for him about August for a year. What did he play? Saxophone. And the piano. Is that Lester Young?
Lester Young's father.
That's Prez.
That's Prez, yeah.
That's Prez.
He's originally from New Orleans. Yeah, originally from New Orleans.

That was the name of the band, the name of the outfit. He had a Varnabors short, it was a little company. He called it a stock company but anybody had their stock in it, I don't know anybody who ever got any dividends out of it. Anyway we traveled around and he had Irma and he had Lester's little brother, Lee Young, he was a terrific dancer and singer and played drums. And this girl Irma played a little trombone and sang and danced. And the old man played the saxophone and the piano. Whenever we get to a house where they had a pretty good piano, we didn't need the saxophone, he'd get out and play the chords. He couldn't take solos too much with those chords on, back you up there. And we played with him, it was just amazing how he could do that. But getting back to Henry, Henry, you know what you're all about, my old lazy daddy, I played with him when I was pretty young. And Henry taught me a lot about leading bands and managing bands and booking and you know, well I'm glad I learned it that way because I wouldn't have what I have to do. Not that I have too much but I probably wouldn't be where I am today but you have that managing, that's where, that's managing the band. Looking out for that money and seeing the boys are taking care fairly and look out for yourself. You've got to look out for yourself too. So as you know darn long time ago we used to, we go out, let's make it round figures, so we go out, we've got five pieces, we make fifty dollars, we split it ten dollars a man right down the middle. You can't stay in business like that. I soon found out you couldn't stay in business like that. But the boys would think you were stealing. They'd think you were stealing. I said, oh, you're always going to have me a band of my own. I'm going to have them to understand, now look, I can't split this money down the middle, I'm going to see that you get a fair salary, I'm going to try to play your scale, whatever union scale is, I'm going to try to stay there above it. But I'm going to always try to make something for myself and I want you to know that. So that's pretty what I've got established. When I came here in San Antonio in 1931, they were still splitting that money down the middle. Well, they were stealing too. They had to steal because there was nowhere in the world you'd operate that band paying expenses and they'd split that money in the middle. Well, when I organized my band I started doing that. But Henry, well Henry even did it too because that was a trend, he would even split it down in the middle. But he was always talking about it and telling me about the things to do what should be done. He had those kinds of eyes, kind of foresight. And of course I knew Sid I was a man I went to the Houston, Houston to play with, wasn't splitting down the middle because when he died he was worth $150,000, probably in cash money together. I know that too. For the fact I saw he had a safe sitting at his house and I knew the combination to it. Always kept me a good fit of whiskey in there though. You know, among all those diamonds and money was that whiskey was there. Thirteen rent houses in Houston, can you imagine that? That's money. Yeah, so I played all around like that, coast to coast, Canada to Mexico, into Mexico. I got here, made that record with Boots and pulled out for Boots myself, that's what I was talking about for myself. I recorded the record, that same record for what's it called, the Tana record company?
Yeah, TNT.
TNT record company. But it didn't go because he didn't have a good distribution, he didn't have a, he couldn't
push the record.
And I wasn't satisfied with the sound of it, he didn't, the audio, he didn't have good audio control on there. Tip된 stuff with stuff with
